note: Chapters of the saga on the home page. `groups` are the scene eras (the `group` column of scene rows in data/ahom.csv) that each chapter collects. `word` is the large Assamese word behind the chapter and `gloss` says what it means. `moments` are scene ids shown in the chapter, `people` are person ids. Edit here, then run: python3 tools/build.py

eras.title: The coming of Sukaphaa
eras.gloss: Charaideo, the first capital and royal burial ground
lead: In 1215 the Tai prince Sukaphaa left Mong Mao with nine thousand followers, priests and two elephants. Thirteen years later he crossed the Patkai hills and came down into Namrup.

He made the Moran and Barahi chiefs his kin by marriage rather than his enemies, set the Burhagohain and Borgohain beside the throne, and in 1253 founded Charaideo, where Ahom kings would lie in their moidams for six centuries. Through three interregnums and a lost prince raised in a Brahmin home, the line held.

eras.title: Swarganarayan’s kingdom
eras.gloss: Garhgaon, the walled capital built in 1540
lead: Suhungmung, the first Ahom king to take a Hindu title, Swarganarayan, doubled the kingdom. He annexed the Chutia lands in 1523, drove the Kacharis back to Dimapur and turned back the armies of Bengal.

When the Bengal general Turbak invaded in 1532, Mula Gabharu took up her fallen husband’s sword and died fighting. Later in 1533 the Ahoms killed Turbak and chased his army back to the Karatoya. Suklenmung built Garhgaon as a fortified capital, and Sukhaamphaa held off the Koch general Chilarai in 1562.

eras.title: Against the Mughal Empire
eras.gloss: Saraighat, where the Mughal fleet was broken in 1671
lead: Pratap Singha and his minister Momai Tamuli Borbarua rebuilt the paik system and created the offices of Borbarua and Borphukan. After years of war the Mughals accepted a frontier on the Barnadi in 1639.

In 1662 Mir Jumla took Garhgaon, but the monsoon and the hill war around Namrup wore his army down, and he died on the way back. Chakradhwaj Singha would not live with the treaty’s shame. His commander Lachit Borphukan retook Guwahati in 1667 and in 1671 broke Ram Singh’s fleet at Saraighat.

eras.title: Six kings in nine years
lead: After Saraighat the ministers held the real power. Debera Borbarua made kings and murdered them; Atan Burhagohain overthrew him; Laluk Sola Borphukan handed Guwahati back to the Mughals in 1679.

To keep a boy-king on the throne, Laluk had the princes maimed, since a maimed prince could never rule. Prince Gadapani escaped into the hills. His wife Joymoti was tortured to death at Jerenga in 1680 rather than say where he was.

eras.title: The Tungkhungia kings
eras.gloss: Rang Ghar, the royal pavilion at Rangpur
lead: Gadapani came out of hiding as Gadadhar Singha, drove the Mughals past the Manas in 1682 and began the Tungkhungia line. His son Rudra Singha built Rangpur and the Joysagar tank and made the Kachari and Jaintia kings his vassals.

Under Siva Singha three queens ruled in turn as Bar Raja. Phuleswari’s persecution of the Moamoria sattra planted the next century’s revolt. Pramatta Singha raised the Rang Ghar in brick, and Rajeswar Singha rebuilt the Kareng Ghar at Garhgaon.

eras.title: The Moamoria risings
eras.gloss: Moamoria, the disciples of the Mayamara sattra
lead: In 1769 the Moamorias took Rangpur and imprisoned Lakshmi Singha. Queen Kuranganayani had the rebel leader killed and the king restored. The second rising, in 1786, drove Gaurinath Singha down the Brahmaputra to Guwahati.

The king asked the East India Company for help, and Captain Welsh’s sepoys pushed the rebels back between 1792 and 1794. The capital moved to Jorhat, Purnananda Burhagohain governed in the king’s name, and the kingdom never recovered its old strength.

eras.title: The days of the Burmese
eras.gloss: The Burmese invasions, remembered as Manor Din
lead: Badan Chandra Borphukan, fleeing his enemies at court, brought a Burmese army into Assam in 1817. Three invasions followed. Chandrakanta, Purandar, Chandrakanta again, then Jogeswar as a puppet: kings were set up and thrown down while the Burmese commander Mingimaha Tilwa held the valley.
When Britain and Burma went to war in 1824, British troops drove the Burmese out. The Treaty of Yandabo, signed in February 1826, gave Assam to the East India Company.

eras.title: The last Swargadeo
eras.gloss: Yandabo, where Assam was signed away
lead: The Ahom nobles had expected their kingdom back. Instead Gomdhar Konwar rose in 1828, and in 1830 Piyali Phukan and Jiuram Dulia Baruah were hanged for plotting to drive the British out.

In 1833 the Company made Purandar Singha a tributary king of Upper Assam and set a tribute he could not pay. In 1838 it removed him and annexed the land, six hundred and ten years after Sukaphaa crossed the Patkai.

reels.title: Sukaphaa leaves Mong Mao
reels.translation: I will go and find a new land.
reels.description: Prince Sukaphaa leaves his ancestral kingdom of Mong Mao following a succession dispute, leading 9,000 followers, noblemen, priests (Deodhais), horses, and two royal war elephants across Upper Burma towards Assam.

reels.title: Sukaphaa crosses the Patkai
reels.translation: Our future lies beyond these hills.
reels.description: Sukaphaa and his vanguard conquer the steep, dense subtropical mountain rainforests of the Patkai Range (Pangsau Pass), outmaneuvering hostile hill tribes and arriving at Khamjang on the border of Assam.

reels.title: Sukaphaa meets the Naga chiefs
reels.description: Descending into Namrup, Sukaphaa establishes firm frontier peace through tactical deterrence and diplomatic accords with eastern Naga chieftains.

reels.title: Sukaphaa, Badaucha and Thakumatha found Bor Axom
reels.translation: From today, we are all one.
reels.description: Sukaphaa adopts an assimilative policy by establishing matrimonial bonds with the indigenous Moran chief Bodousa and the Borahi king Thakumtha, marrying local princesses and integrating them into court governance.

reels.title: Sukaphaa feasts with the Moran and Borahi
reels.description: Sukaphaa adopts an assimilative policy by establishing matrimonial bonds with the indigenous Moran chief Bodousa and the Borahi king Thakumtha, marrying local princesses and integrating them into court governance.

reels.title: Sukaphaa in the new rice fields
reels.description: Introduction of advanced Tai hydraulic techniques, dyke bunding, canal irrigation, and deep-water transplanted Sali rice, producing an agricultural surplus.

reels.title: Sukaphaa’s road to Charaideo
reels.description: In 1253 CE, Sukaphaa establishes the permanent royal capital at Charaideo (Che-Rai-Doi), consecrated with sacred Tai Phuralong rituals and ancestral invocations.

reels.title: Sukaphaa on the throne
reels.description: Convening of the sovereign assembly at Charaideo; state administration organized with local leaders integrated, establishing a harmonious multi-ethnic polity.

reels.title: Sukaphaa plants the royal banner
reels.translation: Here will be our capital: Charaideo.
reels.description: In 1253 CE, Sukaphaa establishes the permanent royal capital at Charaideo (Che-Rai-Doi), consecrated with sacred Tai Phuralong rituals and ancestral invocations.

reels.title: Charaideo, Sukaphaa’s capital
reels.description: In 1253 CE, Sukaphaa establishes the permanent royal capital at Charaideo (Che-Rai-Doi), consecrated with sacred Tai Phuralong rituals and ancestral invocations.

reels.title: Sukaphaa’s last words
reels.description: Upon Sukaphaa's demise in 1268 CE, the tradition of building subterranean vaulted brick/stone chambers covered by hemispherical earthen mounds (Moidams) begins at Charaideo.

reels.title: Suteuphaa takes the throne
reels.description: Sukaphaa's eldest son assumes the golden throne and addresses the council of ministers to set aggressive policies for western border expansion.

reels.title: Suteuphaa on the Dikhou frontier
reels.description: Ahom expanding settlements encounter the Kachari Kingdom's eastern outpost along the Dikhou River.

reels.title: Suteuphaa’s treaty with the Kachari king
reels.description: Suteuphaa sends envoys to avoid destructive protracted war, initiating bilateral talks with the Kachari monarch.

reels.title: The Naga clans conspire
reels.description: Highland Naga chieftains withhold promised tributes and plot coordinated raids on Ahom valley villages.

reels.title: The Naga chiefs submit to Suteuphaa
reels.description: Defeated Naga chiefs travel to the royal court at Charaideo to kneel, submit oaths of loyalty, and pay tribute in salt, iron, and cloths.

reels.title: Sukhaangphaa marches on Kamata
reels.description: King Sukhangphaa leads an offensive against Raja Durlabhanarayana of Kamata, seeking westward expansion into Lower Assam.

reels.title: Sukhaangphaa weds Rajani of Kamata
reels.description: Peace concluded by the marriage of Kamata Princess Rajani (Durlabhanarayana's daughter) to Sukhangphaa, sealing durable inter-kingdom peace.

reels.title: The birth of Chao Pulai
reels.description: A reconstructed scene of the birth of Prince Chao Pulai, linking the Kamata and Ahom royal families.

reels.title: Sukhaangphaa names his son Chao Pulai
reels.description: A reconstructed scene of the birth of Prince Chao Pulai, linking the Kamata and Ahom royal families.

reels.title: Chao Pulai’s secret pact with Kamata
reels.description: Chao Pulai disputes the succession of his half-brother Sukhrangphaa and conspires with maternal Kamata envoys for military support.

reels.title: Sukhrangphaa makes Chao Pulai governor of Sadiya
reels.description: King Sukhrangphaa invests Chao Pulai with governorship of the critical eastern frontier outpost of Sadiya.

reels.title: The ministers keep the empty throne
reels.description: With no acceptable heir after Sukhrangphaa's death, the throne stays empty for five years and the Burhagohain and Borgohain rule. It is the first of three interregnums before 1397.

reels.title: Sutuphaa meets the Chutia king on the Safrai
reels.description: King Sutuphaa meets the Chutia monarch on the Safrai river for joint festivities and peace negotiations to resolve frontier friction.

reels.title: The Burhagohain and Borgohain rule
reels.description: Following Sutuphaa's treacherous assassination, the Burhagohain and Borgohain rule jointly for four years due to the absence of an acceptable adult royal prince.

reels.title: Tyao Khamti marches on the Chutias
reels.description: Nandi and Satyanarayana rule the Chutia kingdom from Sadhayapura (Sadiya), the earliest Chutia kings known from inscriptions. Tyao Khamti's campaign against them fails.

reels.title: Mula Gabharu’s last battle
reels.description: After her husband Phrasengmung Borgohain is killed by Turbak's army, Princess Mula Gabharu leads women warriors into battle and is killed with five companions. Her death rallies the Ahom army.

reels.title: The pregnant queen is cast adrift
reels.description: While King Tyao Khamti is away battling Chutias, his jealous Chief Queen falsely accuses the beloved younger queen and sentences her to be cast adrift on a raft down the Brahmaputra.

reels.title: Prince Sudangphaa is born at Habung
reels.description: The banished pregnant queen washes ashore at Habung and is sheltered by a pious Brahmin family; she gives birth to prince Sudang before passing away.

reels.title: Sudangphaa takes the throne
reels.src: media/reels/clean2/03_Sudangpha_ascends_throne_singari gharat utha niti and hindu asar niti.mp4
reels.description: Grand accession ceremony where Prince Sudang ascends the throne taking the Tai title Chao Siu-Dang-Pha.

reels.title: The feast trap for the Tipam conspirators
reels.description: Early in his reign the Tipam chiefs plot against the young king. Sudangphaa invites the conspirators to a feast and has them killed.

reels.title: Sudangphaa and the Bhuyan marriage alliance
reels.description: Sudangphaa secures stability across the north bank by establishing marriage ties with powerful Baro-Bhuyan chieftains.

reels.title: The boundary treaty at Nongnyang Lake
reels.description: Ahom and Mong Kawng envoys swear a treaty by Nongnyang lake fixing the Patkai range as the border between the two kingdoms. The boundary holds for centuries.

reels.title: The Tangshu raids on the lowlands
reels.description: Tangshu Naga warriors raid eastern border villages, looting grain stores and capturing lowland subjects.

reels.title: The battle against the Kacharis
reels.description: Ahom forces clash fiercely with Kachari armies near the Dikhou; Ahom army suffers a tactical reverse leading to temporary tribute concessions.

reels.title: Peace with the Kacharis
reels.description: Suhenphaa concludes peace with the Kachari king through tribute of royal princesses and elephants, stabilizing the southern flank.

reels.title: The assassination of Suhenphaa
reels.src: media/reels/clean2/10_Muder of suhenpha by kareng labour.mp4
reels.description: Turung palace laborers conceal weapons and spear King Suhenphaa to death inside the palace under cover of darkness.

reels.title: The exiled queen reaches a Naga village
reels.description: Due to malicious palace gossip, Supimphaa banishes his pregnant queen to the village of a loyal Naga chief.

reels.title: Konseng is born in the Naga hills
reels.src: media/reels/clean2/12_Kongsen borpatra gihain born in naga hills.mp4
reels.description: The exiled queen gives birth to prince Konseng among the Nagas, raised in mountain traditions before returning to court.

reels.title: Konseng becomes Barpatragohain
reels.description: Suhungmung creates a third great ministerial post—the Barpatragohain—elevating Konseng to equal rank with Burhagohain and Borgohain.

reels.title: Suhungmung adopts the title Swarganarayan
reels.description: Suhungmung officially assumes the Sanskrit title 'Swarganarayan' (Lord of Heaven), introducing the Saka calendar into state epigraphy.

reels.title: Suhungmung orders a count of fighting men
reels.description: Suhungmung orders the first recorded survey of the kingdom's adult men, the base of the later paik militia system.

reels.title: The Ahom banner rises at Sadiya
reels.description: Chutia forces routed at Chandangiri; Sadiya annexed into the Ahom Empire; office of Sadiya-Khowa Gohain instituted; firearms and copper-plate treasures acquired.

reels.title: Suhungmung commands the river campaign
reels.description: Ahom Bachari war-boats and rowers maneuver against enemy rivercraft with bowmen and bow mounted swivel-guns.

reels.title: The army marches toward Dimapur
reels.description: After five years of war, the Kachari king Khunkhara's army is beaten and its commander killed. The Ahoms chase him to his capital Dimapur; he flees, and Suhungmung installs Detsung as Kachari king.

reels.title: Soldiers patrol the ruins of Dimapur
reels.description: The vassal Kachari king Detsung revolts. The Ahoms pursue him to Jangmarang and kill him; Dimapur is abandoned and the Kacharis move their capital to Maibong. Ahom rule now reaches the Kolong river.

reels.title: Mula Gabharu leads the charge
reels.description: After her husband Phrasengmung Borgohain is killed by Turbak's army, Princess Mula Gabharu leads women warriors into battle and is killed with five companions. Her death rallies the Ahom army.

reels.title: The assassination of Suhungmung: the palace
reels.description: The great king Suhungmung is stabbed in his sleep by his servant Ratiman. His son Suklenmung and a Kachari queen are suspected of the plot.

reels.title: The assassination of Suhungmung: the servant
reels.description: The great king Suhungmung is stabbed in his sleep by his servant Ratiman. His son Suklenmung and a Kachari queen are suspected of the plot.
